source.title: Scaling Laws for the Value of Individual Data Points in Machine Learning
source.authors: Ian Covert; Wenlong Ji; Tatsunori B. Hashimoto; James Zou

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies how individual natural-data points affect test loss and data selection. It does not test the listed versions about random-label memorization, width, architecture, optimizer, batch size, dropout, generalization measures, or removal of memorized examples.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-accuracy changes after adding points selected by different methods. These results concern dataset selection and marginal contributions, not any listed claim version. Cited work on data valuation is not extracted as this study's result.
record.test_reason: The study tests individualized scaling laws for contributions to held-out loss and methods for selecting additional training data. None of V1–V8 is tested. In particular, contribution to population loss is not memorization measured by a point's effect on predicting its own label, and adding high-value points does not test V8's removal intervention.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors find approximate power-law decay in expected individual contributions, with heterogeneous exponents across points, and show that size-specific selection can improve accuracy. They caution that selection ignores current dataset contents and interactions among selected points, and that experiments use simple models and small datasets.
record.recipe_differences: The study estimates natural-data marginal contributions and selects points to add; it does not use the interventions or measurements in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The selected points' test-accuracy improvement varies with preceding dataset size and dataset; Scaling 100 performs best at size 100 in the reported comparisons, while Scaling 1000 performs well at size 1000.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding 20 selected points changes test accuracy differently depending on dataset size and selection method. Scaling 100 gives the largest mean improvement at size 100; at size 1000, Scaling 1000 and Shapley generally outperform Scaling 100.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The usefulness of additional training examples depends on the current dataset size; size-specific contribution estimates can improve data selection.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235, 2024
record.problems: Experiments use relatively simple models and small-scale datasets; the authors identify possible interaction effects among selected points and say their selection approach does not account for the contents of the current dataset. The theory requires strong regularity assumptions and does not make precise predictions for practical scaling parameters.
record.rows_left_out: No reported point-addition table rows omitted. Other scaling-law fit, parameter-correlation, data-valuation-estimator, and variance-fit results do not measure any listed claim version or the test-accuracy effect of adding selected points.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Test error as width increases beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks trained from scratch and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization under different tuning regimes.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Effects of adding or removing dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Ranking examples by self-label memorization and comparing removal with equally sized random removal.

record.verdict_notes: All 24 numerical improvements match Tables 5–6; they are percentage-point changes, with standard deviations over 1000 repetitions. Their states cannot determine any listed version. The record's claim that no point-addition rows were omitted is incorrect: Appendix C.4, Tables 7–8, reports adding 50 points at preceding sizes 200 and 2000. These results also fit no listed version, so they do not require a version-bearing missing entry. Random selection has the largest mean gain for MiniBooNE at size 200.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and generalization on natural labels.
Width beyond interpolation and test error.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and tuning conditions.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other generalization measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
